patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Right-sided nosebleed for 40 minutes that will not stop
background: Recently started clarithromycin for a chest infection
Lives in Brixton with his wife; central heating on high

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely source of bleeding?' or 'most likely cause?': anterior bleeds come from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), posterior bleeds in the elderly from the sphenopalatine artery, and recurrent bleeds point to anticoagulants, HHT or liver disease.

points: Desmond, 73, has had a **right nosebleed** for 40 minutes.
Blood mainly from the **front** of his right nostril.
Takes **warfarin** for AF; started **clarithromycin** 4 days ago.
Dry air at home; he admits picking at a crust.

steps.lead: Desmond's blood is coming from the front of the septum: an **anterior** bleed from **Little's area**, usually milder than a posterior one.

steps.title: Anterior vs posterior epistaxis
head: Feature
Anterior

steps.q: Which factor most explains why Desmond's bleed is so hard to stop?
steps.r: **Clarithromycin** inhibits warfarin metabolism (CYP3A4), raising the INR. **Anticoagulants** are a key cause of difficult or recurrent epistaxis.

steps.lead: Desmond has three common causes: **nose picking, dry air and an anticoagulant**. If bleeds kept recurring, think **HHT** or **liver disease** and check LFTs.

points: He is spitting out blood that runs down his throat.
Looks pale; still alert and talking.
No telangiectasia on lips or tongue.

steps.lead: Desmond's swallowed and spat blood shows the risks: **anaemia, aspiration and airway obstruction**. Instability would mean **resuscitation** and **urgent ENT**.

steps.text: Recurrent nosebleeds plus **telangiectasia** on the lips, tongue or fingertips and a family history means **HHT (Osler-Weber-Rendu)**.
Do not assume a bleed in an elderly patient is posterior just because of age. Look: blood from the **front** with a visible point on the septum is **anterior**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': epistaxis is a clinical diagnosis made by anterior rhinoscopy; bloods (FBC, and clotting if anticoagulated) are for severe bleeding.

steps.q: Bleeding has slowed with pressure. How do you find the source?
steps.r: **Anterior rhinoscopy** (headlight and Thudichum speculum) is the gold standard to see an anterior bleeding point.

steps.lead: With a headlight and speculum, Desmond's **anterior rhinoscopy** shows a bleeding vessel on the right **anterior septum**.

steps.title: Desmond's bloods
steps.text: Hb dropping and a **supratherapeutic INR**: the clarithromycin interaction.

steps.lead: Desmond's bleed is prolonged, so a **full blood count** is sent. Because he is on warfarin, check the **INR** too.

visual.title: Desmond's INR
visual.label: Desmond 4.6
visual.caption: Clarithromycin pushed his INR above range; discuss holding or reducing warfarin.

steps.text: Imaging is not part of routine epistaxis work-up. It is a **clinical diagnosis** confirmed by looking: rhinoscopy, then nasal endoscopy by ENT if posterior.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' or 'next step?': first aid (lean forward, pinch the soft part for 10 to 20 minutes), then vasoconstrictor, cautery if a point is visible, anterior packing, then ENT for posterior packing or sphenopalatine artery ligation.

points: Firm pinch of the **soft part** of the nose for 15 minutes.
Ice pack in his mouth; spits out blood, does not swallow.

steps.lead: Desmond gets first aid properly: **lean forward, pinch the soft part** for 10 to 20 minutes, then a **phenylephrine** spray when it keeps oozing.

steps.title: Epistaxis escalation ladder
nodes: First aid: lean forward, pinch soft part 10–20 min
Fails or no point seen → anterior pack (Rapid Rhino, Merocel)
Still bleeding → ENT: endoscopy, posterior packing
steps.caption: Move one rung at a time.

steps.q: A bleeding point is now visible on Desmond's anterior septum. What next?
steps.r: A **visible** point is cauterised with **silver nitrate**. Packing is for failed cautery or no visible point.

steps.lead: Desmond's point is cauterised, but it oozes again within minutes, so a **Rapid Rhino anterior pack** goes in.

visual.title: Desmond in ED
visual.caption: Pack controls the bleed; pulse settles as anxiety and blood loss stop.

steps.lead: If Desmond kept bleeding despite the pack, suspect a **posterior** source: ENT for **nasal endoscopy** and possible **posterior packing**.
Only if everything fails does Desmond go to theatre for **sphenopalatine artery ligation**.
Once the pack is out and the bleed has settled, Desmond uses **Naseptin** cream to prevent recurrence (check he has no **peanut** allergy).

steps.text: Warfarin: treat the bleed, then review the INR and the interacting drug. Do not reverse anticoagulation routinely for a controlled anterior bleed.

science.exam: Expect applied anatomy: which plexus or artery bleeds, which carotid systems feed Little's area, and why posterior bleeds are worse.

steps.lead: Desmond bled from **Kiesselbach's plexus**: superficial vessels from both the **internal and external carotid** systems meeting on the anterior septum.

steps.title: Arteries feeding Kiesselbach's plexus
nodes: Meet on the anterior septum: Little's area

steps.q: Which artery is the source of most posterior epistaxis?
steps.r: The **sphenopalatine artery**, a terminal branch of the **maxillary** artery, supplies the posterior nasal cavity.

steps.lead: A posterior bleed would come from Desmond's **sphenopalatine artery**: higher volume, hard to see, and commoner at his age.
Desmond's **warfarin** impairs clotting, so a small septal vessel keeps bleeding. In **HHT**, the vessels themselves are fragile.
Desmond's pack worked by **tamponade**. If a pack fails, the source is usually further back or a bigger vessel: hence ligation.

glossary.Little's area: The anterior-inferior nasal septum where Kiesselbach's plexus lies; source of most nosebleeds.
glossary.Kiesselbach's plexus: A network of superficial arteries on the anterior septum from internal and external carotid branches.
glossary.anterior epistaxis: Bleeding from the front of the nose, usually Little's area; typically mild.
glossary.posterior epistaxis: Bleeding from the back of the nasal cavity, usually the sphenopalatine artery; typically severe.
glossary.sphenopalatine artery: Terminal branch of the maxillary artery supplying the posterior nasal cavity.
glossary.maxillary artery: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery.
glossary.anterior ethmoidal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid) supplying the upper anterior nose.
glossary.greater palatine artery: Maxillary artery branch reaching the anterior septum through the incisive canal.
glossary.superior labial artery: Facial artery branch supplying the upper lip and anterior septum.
glossary.watershed: An area supplied by the overlapping ends of two arterial systems.
glossary.anastomosis: A connection between two blood vessels.
glossary.HHT: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia: autosomal dominant fragile vascular malformations causing recurrent bleeds.
glossary.Osler-Weber-Rendu disease: Another name for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
glossary.telangiectasia: Small dilated blood vessels visible on skin or mucosa.
glossary.anticoagulants: Drugs that reduce clotting, such as warfarin or apixaban.
glossary.warfarin: Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant monitored with the INR.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio: measures warfarin effect; target 2 to 3 for AF.
glossary.clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic that inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR.
glossary.rhinoscopy: Looking inside the nose with a light and speculum.
glossary.anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of the front of the nasal cavity with a headlight and speculum.
glossary.Thudichum speculum: Small metal speculum used to open the nostril for examination.
glossary.nasal endoscopy: Examination of the nasal cavity with a rigid camera, done by ENT.
glossary.phenylephrine: Alpha-1 agonist vasoconstrictor used as a nasal spray.
glossary.vasoconstrictor: A drug that narrows blood vessels.
glossary.silver nitrate cautery: Chemical cautery stick applied to a visible bleeding vessel to seal it.
glossary.cautery: Sealing a bleeding vessel with heat or chemicals.
glossary.nasal packing: Material placed in the nose to compress a bleeding vessel.
glossary.Rapid Rhino: An inflatable anterior nasal pack for bleeds not stopped by simple pressure.
glossary.Merocel: A compressed sponge nasal pack that expands with fluid.
glossary.posterior packing: Pack or balloon placed at the back of the nasal cavity for posterior bleeds.
glossary.tamponade: Stopping bleeding by direct pressure on the vessel.
glossary.sphenopalatine artery ligation: Endoscopic surgical tying or clipping of the sphenopalatine artery for refractory epistaxis.
glossary.Naseptin: Chlorhexidine and neomycin nasal cream to prevent recurrence; contains peanut (arachis) oil.
glossary.aspiration: Inhaling blood or fluid into the airway.
glossary.haemodynamic instability: Low blood pressure or high pulse showing the circulation is failing.
